vignette:
Aarav was 46, married, and worked as a software engineer, a role that had once suited the steady concentration and long stretches at a screen that his life seemed to require. Before the incident, he described himself as someone who enjoyed small, ordinary moments of ease: sitting with his spouse after work, reading quietly, or feeling briefly settled on a weekend morning. After the police violence he experienced, even those moments became complicated. He had been walking home in the early evening when a confrontation with police escalated abruptly and violently. He spoke of it in fragments, with long pauses and a visible effort to keep his account ordered, yet the story repeatedly broke apart. Even now, he said he could not give a clear, continuous account of what happened, not because he had forgotten everything, but because the memory would not stay in one place long enough to be told. At times he felt the event as a rush of emotion with no image attached, as if the fear, humiliation, and helplessness arrived all at once in his body before any scene could fully form. If he began to think about that night too directly, he found himself pushing it away before he could complete the recollection, as though stopping short were the only way to keep from being overwhelmed.

In the weeks and months that followed, Aarav found that certain situations could bring back that same charged state without warning. Feeling happy or relaxed was one of the most unsettling. He had expected relief to be comforting, but instead moments of ease could suddenly feel unsafe, as if letting down his guard left him exposed. A quiet dinner with his spouse, a pleasant stretch of an afternoon, even the rare sense that nothing bad was happening could prompt an immediate tightening in his chest and an uneasy scan of the room, as though something might be about to break that calm. Confrontations were similarly difficult. Any conflict, even a minor disagreement at work or a tense exchange in public, pulled him back toward the sense of danger he associated with that night, and he found himself bracing as soon as voices sharpened. He became especially unsettled by people cycling. Seeing cyclists pass on the street or near the office would catch his attention sharply; he would watch them until they were gone, alert to movement and direction in a way that felt automatic rather than chosen. He could not easily explain why cycling had become so potent for him, only that it now stood out as something to monitor.

Aarav also described a strong bodily response when something reminded him of the event. The reaction could come on quickly and intensely, with his heart racing and his body jolting into a state of readiness before he had time to think. In those moments he became preoccupied with where he sat and how protected he felt. At restaurants, in meeting rooms, on public transit, or even in the office kitchen, he would choose his seat carefully, preferring positions that let him see the room and avoid being boxed in. He did this without drawing attention, but it had become a persistent habit, and he noticed how much time he spent arranging himself to feel safer. He was also constantly watching other people for signs that they might harm him. This was not a casual habit but a practiced vigilance: in elevators, on sidewalks, in the building lobby, and around the office, he found himself reading faces, posture, and tone for any hint of threat. He had come to believe that the world’s rules could not be trusted in the way they once had; what happened to him had shattered his sense of how things work, and he now believed that you could never know who might harm you. That belief sat alongside another, more painful conviction: that other people could somehow see what had happened to him just by looking at him. He felt marked by it, as if the experience had left visible evidence on his face or body that strangers could detect.

Over time, these changes altered how Aarav moved through his daily life and work. As a software engineer, he could still do his job, but he described spending more energy on where he positioned himself in shared spaces than on the ease he once took for granted. He noticed himself arriving early to choose a seat that felt safer and avoiding standing too close to people he did not know well. At home, his spouse saw the difference in how guarded he had become, and Aarav felt embarrassed by the sense that he was no longer fully legible to others. What finally brought him to seek help was the accumulation of these experiences and the fear that he was becoming trapped in a life organized around scanning, bracing, and avoiding. He wanted relief from the feeling that he had been permanently changed in a way others could see, and he was most afraid that if he continued like this, he would never again be able to experience happiness or safety without immediately fearing what might come next.
